title: How I automate my own job at Hugging Face using agents — Niels Rogge, Hugging Face
talk_summary: Niels Rogge describes automating Hugging Face community-science outreach with a deterministic nightly cron workflow (plain Python + LLM API calls, no agent framework) that opens GitHub issues/PRs, then a second, more autonomous Claude Agents SDK agent (GLM 5.2 via HF inference providers, deployed on Modal batch containers) that handles follow-ups on those issues. He emphasizes starting simple, tracing with LangFuse, evaluating to avoid slop, and that a single CLI + skill + sandbox is often all an agent needs.

takeaways.technique: Deterministic workflow over autonomous agent for high-volume, well-understood tasks
takeaways.what_they_do: For the nightly paper-scanning job he built a fixed pipeline of LLM API calls in plain Python with no agent framework, run as a cron job, because the steps were known and predictability mattered.

takeaways.technique: Batch fan-out: one container per unit of work
takeaways.what_they_do: He deploys the follow-up agent on Modal's batch processing, spinning up many parallel containers where each container runs exactly one agent loop for one GitHub issue.
takeaways.evidence_quote: they allow you to spin up a massive amount of containers all in parallel. Every single container is basically one agent loop that is processing one GitHub issue

takeaways.technique: One CLI + one skill + sandbox is enough
takeaways.what_they_do: The autonomous follow-up agent only needs Bash as a tool, the Hugging Face CLI, and a skill wrapping that CLI; he reports replacing thousands of lines of custom code with this.
takeaways.evidence_quote: they only need a single CLI, which is the Hugging Face CLI. They need a single skill, the Hugging Face CLI skill, and a sandbox
takeaways.numbers: replaced thousands of lines of custom code with ~200 lines of skill (citing Cursor's 12,000→200 line example)

takeaways.technique: Swap closed models for cheap open models behind a unified provider
takeaways.what_they_do: He moved the follow-up agent from Claude to GLM 5.2 served through Hugging Face inference providers (OpenAI/Anthropic-compatible), citing benchmark parity at lower cost.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Post-training bench is another one where it actually beats Opus 4.8 and it's cheaper. So, yeah, there's no reason not to use GLM
takeaways.numbers: claims GLM 5.2 beats Opus 4.8 on Post-training bench and is cheaper

takeaways.technique: Eval before scaling outreach to avoid slop
takeaways.what_they_do: He explicitly points to Hamel Husain's LLM Evals FAQ as the guardrail against agents spamming low-quality issues, and tracks quality via LangFuse traces (inputs, outputs, prompts, cost, latency).
takeaways.evidence_quote: a blog post that I highly recommend, if you want to avoid that your agent is just posting slop, is um the LLM Evals FAQ
takeaways.numbers: only 2 negative comments out of thousands of issues created

takeaways.technique: Scheduled cron supply of work instead of idle agents
takeaways.what_they_do: A nightly cron job generates hundreds of units of work (GitHub issues/PRs) so the follow-up agents always have a queue; he invokes the follow-up batch on demand via a Cursor skill.
takeaways.evidence_quote: it's a simple cron job. So, cron is just something that runs regularly. In my case, I run it once every night
takeaways.numbers: hundreds of GitHub issues created per night
